etymology: From the Middle English cruse, a small earthen pot or flask, kin to the Old Norse krús and the German Krause; a little vessel for holding oil, water, or honey — the smallest container in the house.
biblical_def: A cruse is a little earthen flask — the smallest vessel of the household, holding oil, or water, or honey. The Authorized Version keeps it for humble things, and the LORD chooses humble things to display His power. At Zarephath a starving widow tells Elijah, “I have not a cake, but an handful of meal in a barrel, and a little oil in a cruse: and, behold, I am gathering two sticks, that I may go in and dress it for me and my son, that we may eat it, and die” (1Ki 17:12). She is at the bottom of her jar and the end of her hope. The word of the LORD comes over that flask: “The barrel of meal shall not waste, neither shall the cruse of oil fail, until the day that the LORD sendeth rain upon the earth” (1Ki 17:14). And so it was — not multiplied into abundance, but never emptied, day by day, for many days (1Ki 17:16). That is the pattern of providence: not a full storehouse but an unfailing bottom. A cruse of water lies at Elijah’s head when he wishes to die (1Ki 19:6), and at Saul’s bolster when David spares the LORD’s anointed (1Sa 26:11). Elisha calls for a new cruse with salt to heal the spring at Jericho (2Ki 2:20). Small vessels, great mercies. The God who fills a cruse is the God who feeds His people to the day of rain.
webster_summary: A small cup, flask, or earthen pot for oil, water, or honey.
webster_full: CRUSE, a small cup or earthen vessel; a bottle or flask for liquids.
From Middle English cruse, kin to Old Norse krús, German Krause.
It names the smallest container of the household, not the storage jar.
The AV distinguishes the cruse of oil from the barrel of meal (1Ki 17:12).
Elisha called for a new cruse for the healing of the waters (2Ki 2:20).
scriptures: And she said, As the LORD thy God liveth, I have not a cake, but an handful of meal in a barrel, and a little oil in a cruse: and, behold, I am gathering two sticks, that I may go in and dress it for me and my son, that we may eat it, and die.
And the barrel of meal wasted not, neither did the cruse of oil fail, according to the word of the LORD, which he spake by Elijah.
And he looked, and, behold, there was a cake baken on the coals, and a cruse of water at his head. And he did eat and drink, and laid him down again.
And he said, Bring me a new cruse, and put salt therein. And they brought it to him.
corruption_summary: The widow’s cruse has been stolen by the prosperity preachers and turned into a promise of return on a donation.
corruption_paragraphs: No text has been more shamelessly abused than 1Ki 17. The seed-faith teachers of the Word of Faith movement — Copeland, Hinn, Dollar, and the long line of televised solicitors behind them — retell Zarephath as a transaction: the widow gave her last meal to the prophet, and therefore her oil never failed; give your last to us, and God is obliged to fill your cruse. This is not exposition but extortion, and it inverts the passage at every point. The widow was not investing; she was obeying a word spoken by the LORD through His prophet in a famine of His own sending. The oil did not multiply into wealth; it merely did not fail. She remained poor to the day of rain, and her son still fell sick and died before the chapter closed. The promise attached to the cruse was the promise of daily sustaining under judgment, not of gain, and the God who gave it was proving His prophet, not paying a subscriber.

What the passage actually teaches is the doctrine of providence in its most searching form. The LORD does not commonly hand His people a full storehouse; He gives a cruse that will not fail. Faith is required not once but every morning, when the flask again looks empty and again pours. So Christ taught His people to pray for daily bread, and so Paul promised that God shall supply all your need — need, not greed — according to His riches in glory by Christ Jesus (Php 4:19). The believer’s security is not in the quantity in the vessel but in the word spoken over it. A man with a full barn and no promise is poor; a widow with a little oil and the word of the LORD is rich, and she outlives the famine.
roots_summary: A small earthen flask for oil or water — the least vessel in the house, and the LORD’s chosen instrument.
roots_lines: Cruse — Middle English for a small earthen pot or flask.
Kin to Old Norse krús and German Krause, a jug.
The AV keeps it for oil (1Ki 17:12), water (1Ki 19:6), and honey (1Ki 14:3).
It is the smallest household vessel, distinct from the barrel and the pitcher.
At Zarephath it becomes the emblem of unfailing daily providence.
usage: The cruse of oil failed not: providence gives an unfailing bottom, not a full storehouse.
A cruse is the least vessel in the house — and the LORD delights to fill the least.
She had a little oil in a cruse and the word of the LORD; that made her rich.

etymology: A compound of bake and meat in its old English sense of food generally (not flesh only); hence baked provisions, pastry-work, the whole craft of the oven. The margin renders the Hebrew “the work of a baker.”
biblical_def: Bakemeats are baked provisions — the pastry and bread-work of a royal kitchen. The word occurs once in Scripture, and it occurs in a dream that ends at a gallows. Joseph, forgotten in the prison house, has just given the chief butler a word of restoration; the chief baker, seeing the interpretation was good, hurries to tell his own dream (Gen 40:16). He had carried three white baskets on his head, “and in the uppermost basket there was of all manner of bakemeats for Pharaoh; and the birds did eat them out of the basket upon my head” (Gen 40:17). Every detail damns him. The baskets are three days. The bakemeats are his office, still borne, still fine, still meant for the king’s table — and the birds are eating them off his head while he stands helpless. Joseph does not soften it: “Yet within three days shall Pharaoh lift up thy head from off thee, and shall hang thee on a tree; and the birds shall eat thy flesh from off thee” (Gen 40:19). Three days later Pharaoh hanged the chief baker, exactly as Joseph had said (Gen 40:22). Two men dream in one night; one is restored and one is executed; the same servant of God speaks the truth to both. The bakemeats teach that a man may be full of the finest work of his hands and still be under sentence, and that the word of God distinguishes between men whom the world cannot tell apart.
webster_summary: Baked provisions; pastry and bread-work — the whole product of the oven.
webster_full: BAKEMEATS, meats or provisions prepared in the oven; baked goods; pastry.
From bake + meat, the older English word for food of any kind.
The AV margin glosses it “the work of a baker, or, cook.”
A KJV hapax, occurring only in the chief baker’s dream (Gen 40:17).
It names the finest output of a royal kitchen, borne in the uppermost basket.
scriptures: And in the uppermost basket there was of all manner of bakemeats for Pharaoh; and the birds did eat them out of the basket upon my head.
When the chief baker saw that the interpretation was good, he said unto Joseph, I also was in my dream, and, behold, I had three white baskets on my head:
Yet within three days shall Pharaoh lift up thy head from off thee, and shall hang thee on a tree; and the birds shall eat thy flesh from off thee.
But he hanged the chief baker: as Joseph had interpreted to them.
corruption_summary: The prison-house chapter is flattened into a tale of a bright young man who kept a good attitude until his luck turned.
corruption_paragraphs: The live misuse of this passage is moralism. Joseph in the prison has become the property of the motivational shelf: keep your outlook high, serve where you are planted, interpret opportunity, and one day you will stand before Pharaoh. But Genesis 40 is not about Joseph’s attitude; it is about God’s revelation and God’s sentence. Joseph himself refuses the credit and names the source — do not interpretations belong to God? The chapter turns on a word from heaven given to a forgotten prisoner, by which one man is spared and another is hanged. To reduce it to a lesson in perseverance is to keep the scenery and lose the judgment, which is precisely the trade the age prefers: a Bible full of encouraging figures and empty of a God who sentences men.

The doctrine to recover is the discriminating word of God. Two officers of the same household commit the same offence, share the same cell, dream on the same night, and receive their answer from the same mouth — and the outcomes are opposite. Nothing in the baker’s conduct distinguished him from the butler; the difference lay wholly in what God had determined and revealed. So it is at the last: two women grinding at the mill, two men in one field, and the dividing word falls between them. And the sentence proved exact to the day, for the word of the LORD never fails by an hour. The bakemeats in the uppermost basket — the finest work of a condemned man’s hands, eaten by birds while he carried them — are a standing picture of every life full of accomplishment and empty of pardon.
roots_summary: Baked provisions — the baker’s craft, and in Scripture the emblem of a condemned man’s finest work.
roots_lines: Bakemeats — bake + meat, the old English word for food generally.
Not flesh-meat: the AV uses meat for any provision, as in meat offering.
The Hebrew margin reads “the work of a baker, or, cook.”
It appears once only, in the chief baker’s dream (Gen 40:17).
Birds devouring the bakemeats prefigured birds devouring the baker (Gen 40:19).
usage: The uppermost basket was full of bakemeats — and the birds were already at them.
Bakemeats is the AV word for the oven’s work, not for flesh.
A man may carry the finest bakemeats and still stand three days from the gallows.

etymology: From parch, to scorch or dry with heat, and corn, the old English word for grain of any kind (wheat or barley, never maize); hence fresh grain roasted at the fire — the harvest field’s ready food.
biblical_def: Parched corn is grain roasted at the fire — wheat or barley taken green from the field, scorched over coals, and eaten on the spot. It is the plainest food in Scripture: harvest food, soldier’s food, the fare of reapers and marching men. The law fenced it about with worship: “ye shall eat neither bread, nor parched corn, nor green ears, until the selfsame day that ye have brought an offering unto your God” (Lev 23:14). Israel might not touch the new crop until the sheaf of firstfruits was waved before the LORD; the first handful belongs to Him who gave the field. When the manna ceased, Israel ate the old corn of the land and parched corn in the selfsame day (Josh 5:11). Jesse sends David to the camp with an ephah of parched corn for his brethren (1Sa 17:17); Abigail loads asses with it to turn away David’s wrath (1Sa 25:18); Barzillai brings it to a fugitive king (2Sa 17:28). But the tenderest use is in Bethlehem’s barley harvest. Boaz calls the foreign widow to the reapers’ table: “he reached her parched corn, and she did eat, and was sufficed, and left” (Rut 2:14). The kinsman’s own hand reaches the food to the stranger; she is filled, and there is more than she can eat. That is the manner of the Redeemer with those who have no claim: He does not scatter a portion, He reaches it, and it is enough and to spare.
webster_summary: Grain roasted at the fire; the ready food of reapers, travellers, and soldiers.
webster_full: PARCHED CORN, grain dried or roasted by fire and eaten without further preparation.
Parch, to scorch or dry with heat; corn, the old English word for grain generally.
Never maize: the AV corn is wheat and barley, the grain of Canaan.
The law forbade eating it before the sheaf of firstfruits was waved (Lev 23:14).
It was harvest fare, camp provision, and the food Boaz reached to Ruth (Rut 2:14).
scriptures: And ye shall eat neither bread, nor parched corn, nor green ears, until the selfsame day that ye have brought an offering unto your God: it shall be a statute for ever throughout your generations in all your dwellings.
Rut 2:14

And Boaz said unto her, At mealtime come thou hither, and eat of the bread, and dip thy morsel in the vinegar. And she sat beside the reapers: and he reached her parched corn, and she did eat, and was sufficed, and left.
And Jesse said unto David his son, Take now for thy brethren an ephah of this parched corn, and these ten loaves, and run to the camp to thy brethren;

Then Abigail made haste, and took two hundred loaves, and two bottles of wine, and five sheep ready dressed, and five measures of parched corn, and an hundred clusters of raisins, and two hundred cakes of figs, and laid them on asses.
corruption_summary: Ruth 2 is retold as a woman’s enterprising rise, with the kinsman-redeemer reduced to a wealthy landowner she managed well.
corruption_paragraphs: The fashionable retelling of Ruth makes the book a study in feminine initiative: a resourceful widow works the system, positions herself in the right field, and secures her own future. Boaz shrinks into the well-off man she handles skillfully, and the parched corn he reaches her becomes a token of her success rather than of his grace. This is a corruption of the book’s whole argument. Ruth is a Moabitess, outside the covenant, propertyless, gleaning at another man’s sufferance under a law that gave her leave to pick up what the reapers dropped. She asks Boaz why she has found grace in his eyes, seeing she is a stranger, and the answer is not her competence but his kindness. The narrative is redemption from the redeemer’s side: he stoops, he covers, he buys, he marries, he raises up the name of the dead. Strip the kinsman-redeemer out of Ruth and nothing is left but a village romance with the gospel removed.

The doctrine to recover is the free kindness of the Redeemer to those with no claim on Him. Boaz does not send Ruth a ration; he calls her to the table with the reapers, reaches the parched corn into her own hand, and gives her so much that she leaves some over. Every motion is a picture of Christ, who does not merely permit sinners to glean at the edges of mercy but seats them at the feast, feeds them from His own hand, and satisfies them past their capacity. And the law over the parched corn stands with it: not a handful of the new harvest might be eaten until the firstfruits were waved before the LORD. Christ is risen, the firstfruits of them that slept; because that sheaf has been presented, His people may eat the harvest without fear.
roots_summary: Fire-roasted grain — harvest fare, camp provision, and the food a redeemer reaches to a stranger.
roots_lines: Parched corn — grain scorched at the fire and eaten at once.
Corn in the AV means grain generally — wheat and barley, never maize.
Forbidden until the firstfruits sheaf was waved before the LORD (Lev 23:14).
It fed the reapers (Rut 2:14), the army (1Sa 17:17), and a fleeing king (2Sa 17:28).
Boaz reached it to Ruth — the redeemer’s own hand to a stranger’s.
usage: He reached her parched corn: the kinsman feeds the stranger from his own hand.
Parched corn is grain roasted at the fire — the plainest food in the Bible.
No parched corn until the firstfruits were waved: the first handful is God’s.

etymology: From the Latin mortarium, which named both the bowl in which substances are pounded and the pounded cement mixed in it; hence in English two things at once — the builder’s cement and the pounding-vessel. The AV spells the cement morter and the vessel mortar.
biblical_def: Morter in the Authorized Version is the builder’s cement — the clay, slime, or lime that binds brick to brick. It appears first at Babel, where men said one to another, let us make brick and burn them throughly, and they had brick for stone and slime for morter (Gen 11:3): the whole tower rests on a mixture of man’s own compounding, and heaven comes down and scatters it. It appears next in Egypt, where the Israelites’ lives were made bitter “with hard bondage, in morter, and in brick, and in all manner of service in the field” (Exo 1:14) — the same trade, now the badge of slavery. In the law it is the plaister of a house cleansed of leprosy (Lev 14:42), and in Ezekiel it becomes the great figure of false ministry: prophets who daub a tottering wall with untempered morter, crying Peace where there is no peace (Eze 13:10), so that the LORD Himself sends the overflowing shower to bring the wall down. The same Latin root gives the household bowl, which the AV spells mortar: “Though thou shouldest bray a fool in a mortar among wheat with a pestle, yet will not his foolishness depart from him” (Pro 27:22). The one vessel gathers the whole doctrine. Providence may pound a man among the wheat, crushing circumstance after circumstance upon him, and he will come out of the bowl the same fool he went in. Pressure does not make a new heart.
webster_summary: A cement of lime, sand, and water for binding brick and stone; also the bowl in which substances are pounded.
webster_full: MORTER, a mixture of lime, clay, or bitumen used to bind bricks and stones in building.
From Latin mortarium, which named the pounding-bowl and the substance pounded in it.
The AV spells the cement morter and the household vessel mortar (Pro 27:22).
At Babel the builders had brick for stone and slime for morter (Gen 11:3).
“Untempered morter” is Ezekiel’s figure for the false prophet’s daubing (Eze 13:10).
scriptures: Exo 1:14
And they made their lives bitter with hard bondage, in morter, and in brick, and in all manner of service in the field: all their service, wherein they made them serve, was with rigour.
And they shall take other stones, and put them in the place of those stones; and he shall take other morter, and shall plaister the house.
Because, even because they have seduced my people, saying, Peace; and there was no peace; and one built up a wall, and, lo, others daubed it with untempered morter:
Though thou shouldest bray a fool in a mortar among wheat with a pestle, yet will not his foolishness depart from him.
corruption_summary: Untempered morter is the trade of every pulpit that daubs over sin with the word Peace.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel names a corruption that never goes out of fashion. A wall is going up badly, and instead of pulling it down the prophets smear it with untempered morter — a plaister with no lime in it, bright on the surface, holding nothing — and they cry Peace where God has declared no peace. That is the business of the flattering ministry in every age: the preacher who will describe every sin except the one his hearers commit, the counsellor who assures a man in rebellion that God accepts him as he is, the church that keeps its numbers by refusing to say the word repent. The LORD’s answer is not correction of the daubing but destruction of the wall: there shall be an overflowing shower, and great hailstones shall fall, and the wall shall come down and the daubers with it. Judgment falls on the wall the false prophets pretended to save.

The other half of the word cuts inward. Solomon puts the fool in the bowl with the wheat and takes the pestle to him, and his foolishness stays. Providence often brays a man — loss upon loss, sickness, failure, the discipline of years — and it grinds the wheat clean while leaving the fool a fool. This is total depravity stated in kitchen terms: the fault is not on the surface of the man, to be pounded off, but in the root of him. Affliction sanctifies the regenerate because the Spirit attends it; on the unregenerate the same affliction only hardens. What Babel needed was not better morter and what the fool needs is not a heavier pestle. Both need what only God can give: a new heart, and a name that is not their own.
roots_summary: The builder’s cement — and, by the same Latin root, the bowl in which the fool is brayed.
roots_lines: Morter — Latin mortarium, both the pounding-bowl and the cement.
AV usage: morter = building cement; mortar = the household vessel.
Babel’s tower was bound with slime for morter (Gen 11:3).
In Egypt morter and brick became the badge of bondage (Exo 1:14).
“Untempered morter” — plaister without lime, the false prophet’s peace (Eze 13:10).
usage: They daubed the wall with untempered morter: a smooth word over a falling house.
Morter and brick were Israel’s bondage before they were Israel’s trade.
Bray a fool in a mortar and you will have bruised wheat and an unchanged fool.

etymology: From the Old French pestel, from the Latin pistillum, “a pounder,” from pinsere, “to beat, to pound”; the heavy club of wood or stone used to bray grain, spice, or drugs in a mortar.
biblical_def: The pestle is the pounder — the heavy club worked by hand in the mortar to bray grain into meal. Israel used it on the manna, going about to gather it, and they “ground it in mills, or beat it in a mortar, and baked it in pans” (Num 11:8). The word itself occurs once, and it occurs as an instrument of hopelessness: “Though thou shouldest bray a fool in a morter among wheat with a pestle, yet will not his foolishness depart from him” (Pro 27:22). Mark what Solomon grants. The pestle works. It reduces wheat to flour without fail; nothing that goes under it comes out unchanged. Put a fool under the same instrument, with the same force, among the very wheat that is yielding, and the wheat becomes meal while the fool remains a fool. The failure is not in the pestle but in the material. Here is the sharp end of total depravity: correction reaches the outside of a man, and folly is bound in the heart of him. Discipline is commanded — the rod of correction shall drive foolishness far from a child (Pro 22:15) — and it is genuinely useful; but it is a means, not a cause, and where God does not attend it with grace it produces a well-beaten fool and nothing more. What the pestle cannot do, God promises to do Himself: “A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you” (Eze 36:26). The pestle grinds; only the Spirit regenerates.
webster_summary: An instrument for pounding or braying substances in a mortar.
webster_full: PESTLE, an implement of wood, stone, or metal for pounding substances in a mortar.
From Old French pestel, Latin pistillum, from pinsere, “to pound.”
Its work is reduction: to bray grain, spice, or drugs to powder.
A KJV hapax, and it appears in a proverb of futility (Pro 27:22).
Israel beat the manna in a mortar before baking it in pans (Num 11:8).
scriptures: Though thou shouldest bray a fool in a mortar among wheat with a pestle, yet will not his foolishness depart from him.
Num 11:8
And the people went about, and gathered it, and ground it in mills, or beat it in a mortar, and baked it in pans, and made cakes of it: and the taste of it was as the taste of fresh oil.
Foolishness is bound in the heart of a child; but the rod of correction shall drive it far from him.
A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh.
corruption_summary: The age believes the pestle: that education, environment, or consequence will grind folly out of a man.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite errors both trust the pestle. The first is the confidence of the modern behaviourist and the modern school: give a man better circumstances, better instruction, better incentives, and the folly will come out of him. Solomon answered that experiment three thousand years before it was funded. Bray him among the wheat, and the wheat gives way and he does not. The second error is the professing Christian version, which is moralism — the notion that a stricter regimen, a harder discipline, or a heavier hand will make a son godly. Scripture commands the rod and honours it; the rod of correction drives foolishness far from a child, and the father who withholds it hates his son. But the rod is a means the LORD is pleased to bless, never a machine that manufactures a new nature. Where God does not open the heart, the strictest household turns out only a disciplined fool.

The doctrine to recover is monergistic regeneration. Foolishness is bound in the heart — not draped over it, not stuck to the surface where a pestle can reach — and the heart is deceitful above all things and desperately wicked (Jer 17:9). Therefore no pressure of providence, no severity of parents, no weight of consequence can dislodge it. God does not undertake to improve the stony heart; He undertakes to take it away and give a heart of flesh. That is a work of sovereign grace, wrought by the Spirit, and it succeeds precisely where every pestle fails. Parents may then use the rod with hope rather than with despair, not because discipline creates life, but because they wield it praying to the God who alone gives it, and who has been pleased to save households through ordinary means faithfully used.
roots_summary: The pounder of the mortar — an instrument that never fails on wheat and always fails on a fool.
roots_lines: Pestle — Old French pestel, Latin pistillum, “a pounder.”
From pinsere, “to beat, to pound” — the same root as piston.
Used on grain, spice, and the manna itself (Num 11:8).
A KJV hapax: the fool brayed with a pestle among wheat (Pro 27:22).
The proverb concedes the instrument works — and still the folly remains.
usage: The pestle never fails on wheat and never succeeds on a fool.
Bray him with a pestle among the wheat: the grain yields, the folly does not.
Discipline reaches the outside of a man; only the Spirit reaches the heart.

etymology: From the Old English sife, kin to the Dutch zeef and the German Sieb; a vessel with a meshed or perforated bottom for separating the fine from the coarse, the grain from the chaff and the dirt.
biblical_def: A sieve is the separating vessel — a rimmed frame with a meshed bottom, shaken until what is worthless falls through and what is wanted remains. Scripture uses it twice in the prophets and once, most tenderly, in the upper room. Isaiah sets it in the hand of God against the nations: His breath comes as an overflowing stream “to sift the nations with the sieve of vanity” (Isa 30:28), and what is shaken out of the sieve of the proud is nothing at all. Amos turns it upon Israel and turns it to comfort: “I will sift the house of Israel among all nations, like as corn is sifted in a sieve, yet shall not the least grain fall upon the earth” (Amo 9:9). The shaking is real — exile, dispersion, the violent agitation of a whole people among the heathen — and yet in all that shaking not one grain is lost. God knows the count of His own. Then in Luke the LORD names the sifter: “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat” (Luk 22:31). Satan asked leave and was granted it, as with Job; the sieve is in the enemy’s hand but the enemy is on the LORD’s leash. And against that shaking Christ sets not a prohibition but a prayer: “But I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not” (Luk 22:32). Peter fell hard; Peter did not fall through. The sieve holds because the Intercessor does.
webster_summary: A vessel with a meshed bottom for separating fine from coarse; a strainer or bolter.
webster_full: SIEVE, a utensil with a bottom of meshed wire or hair, for separating flour from bran or grain from refuse.
From Old English sife, kin to Dutch zeef and German Sieb.
Its office is separation by agitation — the shaking is the whole work.
Amos makes it the figure of Israel’s dispersion with none lost (Amo 9:9).
Isaiah calls God’s judgment on the nations the sieve of vanity (Isa 30:28).
scriptures: Amo 9:9
For, lo, I will command, and I will sift the house of Israel among all nations, like as corn is sifted in a sieve, yet shall not the least grain fall upon the earth.

And his breath, as an overflowing stream, shall reach to the midst of the neck, to sift the nations with the sieve of vanity: and there shall be a bridle in the jaws of the people, causing them to err.
And the Lord said, Simon, Simon, behold, Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat:
But I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not: and when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren.
corruption_summary: The sifting of Peter is quoted to prove that a true believer may be shaken clean out of grace.
corruption_paragraphs: Luk 22:31 is a favourite proof text for the Arminian and the revivalist alike: Satan sifts, therefore the saint may be lost. But the verse cannot be read without the one that follows it, and the two together are among the strongest statements of preservation in Scripture. Christ does not say, I have warned thee to hold on; He says, I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not. The outcome is settled in the Intercessor’s petition before the sifting begins, and He adds what Peter will do afterward — when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren — announcing the restoration before the denial. Satan got exactly what he asked for and still lost. A second misuse runs the other way: men now describe their own drift from the faith as a sifting, as though abandoning doctrine were a work of God upon them. Amos and Luke both make sifting the removal of what was never wheat.

The doctrine to recover is the perseverance of the saints, and the peculiar comfort in Amos’s image. God says He will shake His people among all the nations — and He does; the shaking is severe, and the vessel is often in the enemy’s hand — yet not the least grain shall fall upon the earth. Not one. Not the smallest, weakest, most easily lost of them. The sieve is designed to lose the dust; it cannot lose the grain, because the God who commanded the sifting numbered the wheat before He began. So the believer under trial should ask not whether he will survive the shaking but what the shaking is doing: the chaff of self-confidence goes, and Peter, who had boasted at the table, comes out of the sieve a man who can feed sheep.
roots_summary: The separating vessel — it exists to lose the refuse and it cannot lose the grain.
roots_lines: Sieve — Old English sife, kin to German Sieb.
It works by agitation: the shaking is the sifting.
Isaiah: the nations sifted with the sieve of vanity (Isa 30:28).
Amos: Israel sifted among all nations, yet not the least grain lost (Amo 9:9).
Luke: Satan sifts Simon as wheat, and Christ prays that his faith fail not.
usage: Not the least grain shall fall: the sieve loses dust, never wheat.
Satan asked to sift Peter, and Christ answered the request with a prayer.
A sieve is made to lose things — which is why God chose the figure for preservation.

etymology: From the Old French gernier, a variant of grenier, from the Latin granarium, “a granary,” from granum, “grain”; hence the storehouse into which the threshed and winnowed corn is finally gathered.
biblical_def: A garner is the grain-store — the sealed house into which the winnowed corn is finally carried when the threshingfloor has done its work. It is a word of endings. John the Baptist sets it in the hand of Christ at the last: “Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire” (Mat 3:12; cf. Luk 3:17). Every term is weighed. The fan is already in His hand. The floor will be purged throughly — not sampled, not partially cleared, but swept to the boards. The wheat is his wheat, His own by election and purchase, and it is gathered in; the chaff is burned with a fire that is not quenched. There is no third heap and no third destination. In the Old Testament the garner is the token of covenant blessing when full and of covenant judgment when empty. David’s prayer for a settled people is “that our garners may be full, affording all manner of store” (Psa 144:13), and Solomon promises the man who honours the LORD with his substance, “So shall thy barns be filled with plenty, and thy presses shall burst out with new wine” (Pro 3:10); while Joel describes a land under the locust in one line — “the garners are laid desolate, the barns are broken down; for the corn is withered” (Joe 1:17). A nation is measured at its storehouse door. And so is a soul: the whole of a man’s life is a growing season, and the harvest ends in one of two places, the garner or the fire.
webster_summary: A granary; a storehouse for threshed grain.
webster_full: GARNER, a granary; a building or room in which grain is stored after threshing.
From Old French gernier, Latin granarium, from granum, “grain.”
It is the last stage of harvest, after reaping, threshing, and winnowing.
Full garners are the emblem of covenant blessing (Psa 144:13).
Christ gathers His wheat into the garner and burns the chaff (Mat 3:12).
scriptures: Mat 3:12
Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.
Luk 3:17
Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and will gather the wheat into his garner; but the chaff he will burn with fire unquenchable.
Pro 3:10
So shall thy barns be filled with plenty, and thy presses shall burst out with new wine.
Joe 1:17
The seed is rotten under their clods, the garners are laid desolate, the barns are broken down; for the corn is withered.
corruption_summary: The garner is kept and the fire is quietly dropped — an ingathering with no second heap.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern handling of Mat 3:12 keeps half a verse. The gathering of the wheat is preached warmly; the unquenchable fire is explained away. Annihilationism, now common among evangelicals who wish to keep the Scriptures and lose the doctrine, says the chaff is consumed and ceases to be, though the text calls the fire unquenchable and not the chaff consumable. Universalism, older and bolder, says the fire is remedial and every sheaf reaches the garner at last — the nineteenth-century universalist euphemism revived in our own age. Both corruptions require that John the Baptist did not mean what he said, and both fail on the plain structure of his sentence: one Man with one fan makes one separation into two heaps with two ends. The dictionary holds the confessional position without apology: eternal conscious punishment for the unredeemed, on the authority of the Christ who first announced it.

The doctrine to recover is the definite and effectual ingathering. Notice whose wheat it is. He gathers his wheat — the grain was His before the fan moved, chosen of the Father, purchased at the cross, and now brought home; the winnowing does not decide the harvest, it reveals it. Notice also that He purges His floor throughly. Not one grain of His is left lying on the boards to be swept out with the chaff, and not one grain of chaff is carried into the garner by mistake. That is a terror to the man who has only ever been chaff, however long he has lain on the church floor; and it is unshakeable comfort to the weakest true believer, who is not gathered because he held on but because he is the Lord’s wheat, and the Lord of the harvest loses nothing.
roots_summary: The granary — the last stop of the harvest, and one of only two destinations for men.
roots_lines: Garner — Old French gernier, Latin granarium, from granum.
The storehouse for threshed and winnowed grain, distinct from the threshingfloor.
Full garners mark covenant blessing (Psa 144:13); desolate ones, judgment (Joe 1:17).
In the Gospels it is the final destination of the wheat (Mat 3:12; Luk 3:17).
Its opposite in the same verse is the fire that is never quenched.
usage: He will gather his wheat into the garner: the harvest ends in a storehouse or a fire.
A garner is the last building the corn ever enters.
He purges His floor throughly — no grain of His is swept out with the chaff.

etymology: A plain English compound of water and pot, rendering the Greek hydria, a standing water-jar. The AV keeps waterpot for this large vessel and reserves pitcher for the carrying-jar of the well — two distinct words for two distinct vessels.
biblical_def: A waterpot is the standing water-jar of a house — a heavy vessel that sits, unlike the pitcher, which is carried on the shoulder to the well. The Authorized Version keeps the two words apart, and John uses the waterpot for both of his great water scenes. At Cana “there were set there six waterpots of stone, after the manner of the purifying of the Jews, containing two or three firkins apiece” (Joh 2:6) — stone, because stone did not contract ceremonial defilement; six, one short of the number of fulness; set there for the endless washing of hands and vessels that the ceremonial law and rabbinic addition required. They are the whole apparatus of purification by ritual, and at the marriage they are standing empty. Christ says, “Fill the waterpots with water. And they filled them up to the brim” (Joh 2:7) — and the water of ceremony becomes the wine of the feast, better than what the governor had tasted first. The old order is not merely supplemented; it is transformed and surpassed by Him, and this beginning of miracles manifested forth His glory, and His disciples believed on Him (Joh 2:11). Two chapters later a Samaritan woman comes to a well with a waterpot of her own and meets the One who gives living water; and when He has told her all things that ever she did, “the woman then left her waterpot, and went her way into the city” (Joh 4:28). She came for water and left the vessel behind. Whoever finds Christ can afford to.
webster_summary: A vessel for holding water; the standing stone or earthen jar of a household.
webster_full: WATERPOT, a vessel for holding or conveying water; a large standing jar.
A compound of water + pot, rendering the Greek hydria.
Distinct in the AV from pitcher, the smaller vessel carried to the well.
The Cana waterpots were of stone, holding two or three firkins apiece (Joh 2:6).
Stone was used because it did not contract ceremonial uncleanness.
scriptures: Joh 2:6
And there were set there six waterpots of stone, after the manner of the purifying of the Jews, containing two or three firkins apiece.
Joh 2:7
Jesus saith unto them, Fill the waterpots with water. And they filled them up to the brim.
Joh 2:11
This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of Galilee, and manifested forth his glory; and his disciples believed on him.
Joh 4:28
The woman then left her waterpot, and went her way into the city, and saith to the men,
corruption_summary: Cana is emptied of its miracle and kept as a symbol — a story about generosity rather than an act of God in a stone jar.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern academic treatment of Joh 2 characteristically declines the event and keeps the meaning: the waterpots become a literary device, the wine a symbol of abundance, and the reader is invited to appreciate the theme without believing that water in six stone jars turned to wine in Galilee about the year 27. This is unbelief wearing the vestments of interpretation. John does not offer a symbol; he reports a sign, dates it, counts the jars, measures their capacity, names the town, and records that the governor of the feast tasted the result and did not know where it came from — the details of a witness, not of an allegorist. Strip the miracle out and the conclusion John draws collapses with it, for he says the disciples believed on Him because His glory was manifested; nobody ever believed on a literary device.

The doctrine to recover is the fulfilment and surpassing of the ceremonial law in Christ. The six waterpots existed for the purifying of the Jews — water poured over hands and cups without end, a washing that had to be repeated because it never reached the conscience. Christ does not overturn the jars; He fills them to the brim and transforms their contents into the wine of the marriage feast. That is the gospel’s relation to the ceremonial law exactly: not contempt for the shadow but its completion in the substance, so that the blood of Christ purges the conscience from dead works where the water of ritual never could. And the Samaritan woman shows the effect on a sinner: she set down the vessel she had come for and ran to tell a town about a Man who told her all things that ever she did.
roots_summary: The standing water-jar — the vessel of ceremonial purifying, filled to the brim and transformed.
roots_lines: Waterpot — water + pot, rendering the Greek hydria.
A standing jar, not the shoulder-borne pitcher of Gen 24 — the AV keeps them distinct.
Six stone jars at Cana, of two or three firkins each — roughly twenty gallons apiece.
Stone was chosen because it did not contract ceremonial defilement.
The Samaritan woman left hers at the well and went to tell the city (Joh 4:28).
usage: Fill the waterpots to the brim: Christ takes the vessels of ceremony and fills them with joy.
A waterpot stands; a pitcher is carried — the AV never confuses the two.
She left her waterpot: what she came to the well for no longer mattered.

etymology: From the Old French pichier, a jug, through Medieval Latin bicarium; in the AV the earthen jar carried on the shoulder or hand to draw water. It is a distinct word from waterpot, the large standing vessel of Joh 2 and Joh 4.
biblical_def: A pitcher in the Authorized Version is the carrying-jar — earthen, shoulder-borne, taken daily to the well. It is never the standing waterpot of John’s Gospel; the AV keeps the two words for two vessels, and the difference is the difference between the jar that goes out and the jar that stays. Abraham’s servant prays at a well in Mesopotamia for a sign, and “behold, Rebekah came out… with her pitcher upon her shoulder” (Gen 24:15); she waters ten camels out of it, and a marriage in the line of promise is settled at a watering-trough. Under Gideon three hundred men carry empty pitchers with lamps hidden inside, and at the trumpet “the three companies blew the trumpets, and brake the pitchers, and held the lamps in their left hands” (Jdg 7:20), and a host flees before broken crockery and burning light. Paul gives the doctrine of it: “we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us” (2Co 4:7). The vessel must break before the light is seen; the weakness of the preacher is the proof of the power. And Solomon uses the same jar for the end of life — “or the pitcher be broken at the fountain, or the wheel broken at the cistern” (Ecc 12:6) — the body failing at the very spring that fed it. Jeremiah uses the same jar for a ruined people, lamenting that the precious sons of Zion, comparable to fine gold, are esteemed as earthen pitchers, the work of the hands of the potter (Lam 4:2). Every pitcher breaks. The question is whether there is light inside when it does.
webster_summary: An earthen jar with a handle, carried for drawing and pouring water.
webster_full: PITCHER, an earthen or metal vessel with a handle, used for holding and pouring liquors.
From Old French pichier, through Medieval Latin bicarium, a drinking jug.
In Scripture it is the well-jar, borne on the shoulder or let down by hand.
Distinct from the AV waterpot, the large standing vessel of Joh 2 and Joh 4.
Gideon’s men hid lamps in empty pitchers and broke them at the signal (Jdg 7:16).
scriptures: And it came to pass, before he had done speaking, that, behold, Rebekah came out, who was born to Bethuel, son of Milcah, the wife of Nahor, Abraham's brother, with her pitcher upon her shoulder.
Jdg 7:20

And the three companies blew the trumpets, and brake the pitchers, and held the lamps in their left hands, and the trumpets in their right hands to blow withal: and they cried, The sword of the LORD, and of Gideon.
Lam 4:2
The precious sons of Zion, comparable to fine gold, how are they esteemed as earthen pitchers, the work of the hands of the potter!
But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us.
corruption_summary: An age that will not have the vessel broken cannot understand why the light was hidden in it.
corruption_paragraphs: The live corruption here is the self-esteem gospel, which teaches that a man’s deepest want is a higher opinion of himself and that the preacher’s office is to supply it. On that reckoning Gideon’s three hundred should have polished their pitchers and displayed them. Paul says the opposite, and says it as the reason for the arrangement: the treasure is put in earthen vessels precisely that the excellency of the power may be of God and not of us. God does not choose weak instruments in spite of their weakness but because of what their weakness will prove when the victory comes. The pulpit that promises the believer he will be strengthened in his own estimation is offering him an unbroken pitcher, and an unbroken pitcher shows no light at all. Christ’s people are pressed, perplexed, persecuted, cast down — and the glory shines out of the cracks.

The doctrine to recover is that God works through means so plainly inadequate that no man can claim the result. Three hundred men with trumpets, lamps, and clay jars; a servant praying at a well and a girl with a jar on her shoulder; a handful of unlearned fishermen sent against the Roman world. In every case the vessel is common and the outcome is impossible, and the sword is the LORD’s before it is Gideon’s. Solomon then sets the same figure over the end of life: the pitcher broken at the fountain, the body giving out at the source that supplied it, dust returning to the earth as it was and the spirit returning unto God who gave it (Ecc 12:7). Every earthen vessel breaks at last. Blessed is the man in whom the breaking only lets out more light.
roots_summary: The earthen well-jar — carried, emptied, and finally broken, that the light within may be seen.
roots_lines: Pitcher — Old French pichier, Medieval Latin bicarium, a jug.
In the AV it is the carrying-jar of the well, borne on the shoulder (Gen 24:15).
It is NOT the AV waterpot, the large standing vessel of Joh 2 and Joh 4.
Gideon’s pitchers hid lamps and were broken to show them (Jdg 7:20).
Ecclesiastes makes the broken pitcher the figure of death (Ecc 12:6).
usage: They brake the pitchers, and the light came out: the vessel must break to shine.
Rebekah came with her pitcher upon her shoulder — and a covenant line was settled.
The pitcher is the well-jar; the waterpot is the house-jar. The AV keeps them apart.

etymology: From the Old English mylen, from the Late Latin molina, from molere, “to grind”; the household hand-mill of two stones, the upper turned upon the nether to grind grain into meal. The AV millstone names the stone; mill names the whole apparatus and the labour at it.
biblical_def: The mill of Scripture is not a building but a pair of stones — the nether stone fixed, the upper turned by hand, usually by two women seated opposite one another, grinding the day’s grain before the day’s bread. It was the lowest and most constant labour of a household, which is why the AV uses it to mark the bottom of a society: the LORD threatens the firstborn of Egypt “from the firstborn of Pharaoh that sitteth upon his throne, even unto the firstborn of the maidservant that is behind the mill” (Exo 11:5). Throne and hand-mill are the two ends of the nation, and judgment reaches both. Israel in the wilderness ground the manna in mills or beat it in a mortar and baked it in pans (Num 11:8) — even bread from heaven was worked by human hands. When Jerusalem fell, the sign of ruin was that “they took the young men to grind” (Lam 5:13), the free man set to the woman’s stone; and blinded Samson turned a Philistine mill in the prison house. The law even fenced the mill about with mercy: no man might take the nether or the upper millstone to pledge, for he taketh a man’s life to pledge (Deu 24:6) — seize a household’s mill and you have seized its bread. Then Christ takes this most ordinary scene and hangs eternity on it: “Two women shall be grinding at the mill; the one shall be taken, and the other left” (Mat 24:41). Two hands on one stone, one destiny apart.
webster_summary: An engine or machine for grinding grain; in Scripture, the household hand-mill of two stones.
webster_full: MILL, a machine for grinding grain and reducing it to meal or flour.
From Old English mylen, Late Latin molina, from molere, “to grind.”
The biblical mill is a hand-mill: a fixed nether stone and a turning upper stone.
The AV millstone names the stone itself; mill names the apparatus and the labour.
Grinding was women’s daily work and, for captives, the badge of servitude (Lam 5:13).
scriptures: Exo 11:5

And all the firstborn in the land of Egypt shall die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh that sitteth upon his throne, even unto the firstborn of the maidservant that is behind the mill; and all the firstborn of beasts.
Two women shall be grinding at the mill; the one shall be taken, and the other left.
Num 11:8
And the people went about, and gathered it, and ground it in mills, or beat it in a mortar, and baked it in pans, and made cakes of it: and the taste of it was as the taste of fresh oil.
Deu 24:6
No man shall take the nether or the upper millstone to pledge: for he taketh a man's life to pledge.
corruption_summary: Two women at a mill have been conscripted into a secret rapture the passage does not teach.
corruption_paragraphs: Mat 24:41 is the standing proof text of dispensational premillennialism — a nineteenth-century novelty of Darby and Scofield unknown to any Reformation confession — which reads the one taken as a believer secretly caught away and the one left as an unbeliever abandoned to a seven-year tribulation. The context will not carry it. The Lord has just compared that day to the days of Noah, when they ate and drank and married until the flood came and took them all away; the taking in the figure He Himself supplies is the taking of judgment, and those left are the preserved. Whichever way the terms are read, the passage teaches one thing plainly and it is not a secret removal: the second coming will be visible as lightning shining from the east unto the west, sudden, and final, and it will fall upon people at their ordinary work with no interval for a second chance.

The doctrine to recover is the ordinariness of the setting and the absoluteness of the separation. Two women sit at one stone, hands on the same handle, grinding the same grain for the same household — nearer to each other than most of us are to anyone — and at that moment the division of eternity passes between them. The last day does not find men in a religious posture; it finds them at the mill, in the field, in the bed. There is no visible difference between the two women that morning, and no one at the mill could have told you which was which; the difference is what God knows and what will then be revealed. That is why Christ closes the passage not with a calendar but with a command: watch therefore, for ye know not what hour your Lord doth come.
roots_summary: The household hand-mill of two stones — the plainest daily labour, and the scene of the last separation.
roots_lines: Mill — Old English mylen, Latin molere, “to grind.”
A hand-mill of two stones, not a building: nether stone fixed, upper stone turned.
Distinct from millstone, which names the stone itself.
Behind the mill = the bottom of the household (Exo 11:5); to grind = servitude (Lam 5:13).
The law forbade taking a mill in pledge — it is a family’s bread (Deu 24:6).
usage: From the throne to the mill: judgment reached both ends of Egypt in one night.
The mill is the hand-mill of two stones, not a building on a stream.
Two women grinding at the mill, one taken and one left — the last day finds men at work.
